The OCEAN assessment collects 12 scale responses (1–5) across five personality dimensions. Each dimension is measured by 2–3 questions. The questions are written in plain first-person language — no psychological terminology is visible to the user. The dimension each question measures is internal only.
I'm drawn to ideas and questions even when they have no practical use.
I tend to notice things — patterns, connections, ideas — that aren’t directly relevant to what I’m doing.
I tend to follow through on things I set for myself even when motivation drops.
When things feel out of control externally, I usually try to control what I can internally.
I often leave things half-finished when motivation drops or something else comes up. [REVERSE SCORED: score = 6 − raw answer before averaging]
When I'm stressed, being around people usually helps me feel better.
I process things better by talking them through than sitting with them alone.
I usually prefer to think things through on my own rather than talk them out with someone. [REVERSE SCORED: score = 6 − raw answer before averaging]
I find it hard to express frustration or disagreement directly to someone I care about.
I tend to keep difficult feelings to myself rather than share them in the moment. [Reframed from original: same construct, observational rather than self-critical framing.]
When I disagree with someone, I usually just say so. [REVERSE SCORED: score = 6 − raw answer before averaging]
My mood can be affected by things that might seem minor to others. [Reframed from original: same construct, less judgmental framing.]
I often replay conversations or situations in my head long after they've happened.
Once a stressful event is over, I can usually move on from it fairly quickly. [REVERSE SCORED: score = 6 − raw answer before averaging]
When I'm anxious I find it hard to identify exactly what I'm anxious about.
I prefer variety and novelty over routine and predictability. [REVERSE SCORED]
I often put off tasks even when I know I shouldn't. [REVERSE SCORED]
I find social situations draining rather than energising. [REVERSE SCORED]
I rarely feel anxious or worried without a clear reason. [REVERSE SCORED]
What a high vs low score actually signals in this context

High (4–5): intellectually curious, drawn to abstract ideas, notices patterns beyond the immediate. Low (1–2): tends to seek certainty and concrete grounding — reflections work better with specifics, less abstraction. Q13 is reverse-scored (preference for novelty = high O).

High (4–5): follows through, self-regulating even under pressure. Low (1–2): may struggle with the daily entry habit — re-engagement prompts matter more; exercises should not feel like tasks. Q14 is reverse-scored (procrastination = low C).

High (4–5): processes by talking, socially energised. Low (1–2): internal processor — do not assume social support is a natural first step in reflections or exercise framing. Q15 is reverse-scored (finding social situations draining = low E).

High (4–5): conflict-avoidant, accommodating, absorbs others' emotional states. Directly relevant to Branch A and C patterns — high agreeableness + high PR is a common suppression combination. Low (1–2): more direct, less likely to people-please.

High (4–5): emotionally reactive, ruminates, difficulty pinning anxiety. Directly relevant to Branch D and distress trajectory. Low (1–2): emotionally stable — reflections can be more direct and less attentive to distress signals. Q16 is reverse-scored (rarely feeling anxious = low N).

This section specifies the complete screen-by-screen flow, interaction design, and UI behaviour for the OCEAN assessment. It is a handoff document for both the designer and the developer — each element is annotated with who owns it.

The OCEAN assessment screen appears immediately after the user completes account creation (email + password, or SSO). It is the first screen the user sees inside the product. There is no welcome screen, no product tour, and no dashboard interstitial between sign-up and this screen.

The transition from account creation to Q1 should feel immediate — not like entering a new section of the app. No loading animation, no 'Welcome to Ingress Within' screen. The first question appears. That is the product experience starting.

Gate condition: show OCEAN screen only when User.onboarding_completed = No AND User.personality_profile_json is empty. If either condition is already true, skip directly to Day 1 entry screen. This prevents re-showing the assessment if a user drops mid-flow and returns.
Each of the 12 questions occupies its own screen. The layout is identical for all 12. No question-specific formatting, imagery, or variation.

Small muted text top-left or top-centre. Format: '3 of 12'. The original decision was number-only (no progress bar), on the rationale that a bar implies something to complete. A 2px thin fill bar has been added alongside the counter in the frontend implementation — using Teal Black fill advancing on answer, not on screen load. If the ‘implies completion’ concern resurfaces in user testing, the bar element can be removed; the N of 12 counter remains either way.

Large, centred, high contrast. Font size significantly larger than body text. Single question only — never two questions on one screen. Max 2 lines at standard mobile width before the text reflows — keep all 12 questions under this limit.

5 options presented as a horizontal row of tappable blocks or circles. No labels on 1–4. Labels only on endpoints: 1 = 'Not like me at all', 5 = 'Very much like me'. Labels appear below the scale, not above.
Muted, small. Not bolded. They should not dominate the visual hierarchy — the question and the scale buttons do.
Tapping a scale option selects it with a visible filled/active state. Tapping another option deselects the previous one. Only one selection per question allowed.

After a selection is made, the screen automatically advances to the next question after a 400ms delay. The delay is intentional — prevents accidental skips and gives a moment of pause between questions. Do NOT require a separate 'Next' button tap.
Not available. Once a question is answered and the next screen appears, the previous response is locked. No back arrow. No swipe-back gesture.
All 12 questions are required. There is no 'Skip' or 'Prefer not to say' option. The submit to backend only fires after Q12 is answered.
After the user selects a response for Q12, the auto-advance fires as usual. Instead of showing Q13 (which doesn't exist), it transitions to a brief loading state while the API call processes.
Raw answers written to User.personality_profile_json. Five dimension scores calculated and written to User record. This happens client-side before the API call fires — scores are available instantly.
Personality summary API call fires with the five scores. Loading state shown to user.
Minimal. One short sentence only, centred on screen: 'One moment.' No spinner animation if avoidable — a subtle fade or pulse on the text is enough. Do not show a percentage or progress indicator.
personality_summary_text written to User record. Screen transitions to Summary Screen (Section 2.4).

If the API call takes longer than 8 seconds or fails: skip the summary screen entirely. Set onboarding_completed = Yes. Route directly to Day 1 entry screen. Do not show an error. The summary is a one-time experience — losing it is preferable to blocking the user.

Do not show the Summary Screen until personality_summary_text is successfully written to the User record. If the user reaches the Summary Screen and the field is empty, the summary text element will render blank — a broken first impression. The API call must complete before the screen transition.
The Summary Screen is shown exactly once. The user will never see this screen or this content again. The design should convey that — quiet, considered, not celebratory.
Text: 'Here's what we noticed.' Medium weight — not bold, not a headline. Slightly larger than body text. Top of the content area, generous space above it.

The AI-generated 2–3 sentence personality summary from personality_summary_text. Larger text size than the header — this is the primary content. No card, no border, no background. Just text with generous white space above and below. Left-aligned, not centred.
Simple 1px horizontal rule below the summary text. Full width. Muted colour — not decorative, just structural.
Below the divider. Smaller, muted colour. Exact copy: 'This shapes how we respond to you. You won't see it again — but it's working in the background.' Do not italicise. Do not add quotation marks.
Full width. Solid fill. Text: 'Continue'. No secondary button. No 'Go back' or 'Edit answers' option.
Sets User.onboarding_completed = Yes. Routes to Day 1 entry screen. No animation — direct transition.

The summary screen should not feel like a result or a reward. It is more like being told something true about yourself before a conversation begins. The visual tone should be calm and direct — no confetti, no congratulations, no product marketing language. White space is doing most of the work here.

The OCEAN assessment repeats every 90 days. The user is not told this is happening — it appears as a silent interruption to the normal entry flow, identical in design to the initial onboarding assessment. The purpose is to allow the profile to converge toward the user’s actual dispositional baseline over time, correcting for bad-day effects and the lower reliability of a 15-item self-report instrument.
current_date >= (last_assessment_date + 90 days) AND onboarding_completed = Yes. Check on every app open, before routing to Day 1 entry screen. If true, route to reassessment instead.

Identical to the initial assessment in every way. Same questions, same scale, same auto-advance, same loading state. No explanation is shown to the user about what this is or why it is happening. No indication that it differs from normal app use. After the final question, the same ‘One moment.’ loading state appears while scores are blended and a new summary is generated.

Running equal-weight average. For each dimension: blended_score = ((current_score × assessment_count) + new_score) / (assessment_count + 1). Apply to all five dimensions. Round to 1 decimal place. Then increment assessment_count by 1. Then write blended scores to the five ocean_ fields. Then write new raw scores to the five ocean_*_latest fields. Then update last_assessment_date to today. All in a single atomic workflow action.

Same API call as Section 4.1, using the newly blended scores. Same prompt. Same 8-second timeout and retry logic (Section 4.7). If it succeeds, personality_summary_text is overwritten with the new summary — this is the only time this field is ever overwritten. If it fails or times out, keep the existing personality_summary_text and continue. Do not surface the failure to the user. Unlike initial onboarding, no summary screen is shown to the user after reassessment — the update is entirely invisible. Route directly to Day 1 entry screen after completion.

All OCEAN data is stored on the User record — not in a separate ExerciseResult record. Rationale: the OCEAN assessment is not a timed exercise that unlocks based on entry count. It is a one-time onboarding event. Storing it on the User record makes it permanently and immediately accessible to every AI prompt without a secondary database lookup.

Long Text. JSON string. Format: {"q1":4,"q2":2,"q3":5,"q4":3,"q5":1,"q6":2,"q7":4,"q8":5,"q9":3,"q10":4,"q11":5,"q12":3}. Written immediately after Q12 is submitted, before the API call fires. Not read by routing logic — exists for audit, quality review, and potential future reanalysis if question set changes. REVERSE SCORING NOTE: Raw answers are stored as-is (1–5 exactly as tapped). The reverse-score transformation for Q9 is applied only at calculation time in Section 3.2 — not to the stored value. This means personality_profile_json always holds the literal user response, which is correct for audit purposes.

Number. One decimal place. Calculation: (q1 + q2 + (6−q13)) / 3. Range 1.0–5.0. Q13 reverse-scored. Written at same time as personality_profile_json. From reassessment 2 onward: blended running average — see Section 3.4.
Number. One decimal place. Calculation: (q3 + q4 + (6−q14)) / 3. Range 1.0–5.0. Q14 reverse-scored.
Number. One decimal place. Calculation: (q5 + q6 + (6−q15)) / 3. Range 1.0–5.0. Q15 reverse-scored.

Number. One decimal place. Calculation: (q7 + q8 + (6 − q9)) / 3. Range 1.0–5.0. Three questions — only dimension averaged across 3. Q9 is reverse-scored: subtract the raw answer from 6 before averaging. A raw answer of 5 (strongly agree ‘I say so directly’) = low agreeableness = score of 1. A raw answer of 1 = high agreeableness = score of 5.
Number. One decimal place. Calculation: (q10 + q11 + q12 + (6−q16)) / 4. Range 1.0–5.0. Q16 reverse-scored.

Long Text. AI-generated 2–3 sentence plain language summary. Written after API call completes. This is the primary downstream field — passed into every subsequent AI prompt as standing context. Regenerated after each reassessment using the updated blended scores. The previous summary is overwritten. See Section 3.4. Regenerated on each reassessment from the updated blended scores.

Number. Integer. Starts at 1 after initial onboarding assessment. Incremented by 1 on each reassessment. Used to calculate running average: new_score = ((old_score × assessment_count) + latest_score) / (assessment_count + 1). After incrementing, reflects total number of assessments completed.
Date. Written immediately after each assessment completes (initial and reassessment). Used to calculate when the next reassessment is due: last_assessment_date + 90 days. Never shown to the user.

Number. One decimal place. The raw score from the most recent assessment only, before blending. Stored for audit and delta analysis. Not used in AI prompts — only the blended ocean_openness field is passed as standing context.
Number. One decimal place. Raw score from most recent assessment. Same audit purpose as ocean_openness_latest.
Number. One decimal place. Raw score from most recent assessment.
Number. One decimal place. Raw score from most recent assessment. Already reverse-scored on Q9 before storage — same transformation as the blended field.
Number. One decimal place. Raw score from most recent assessment.

All five dimension scores are calculated client-side immediately after Q12 is submitted, before the API call fires. In Bubble, this means a workflow that runs on the Q12 submission button (or auto-advance trigger) and makes a single 'Make changes to current User' action with all five calculations in one step.

Do all five score calculations in a single 'Make changes to User' workflow action — not five separate actions. This ensures the scores are written atomically. If the workflow is split into five sequential actions and one fails mid-way, you will have partial data that silently passes incorrect context into AI prompts.
Reverse-scored items — apply (6 − raw_value) before including in dimension average: Q9 (Agreeableness): scored = 6 − q9_value Q13 (Openness): scored = 6 − q13_value Q14 (Conscientiousness): scored = 6 − q14_value Q15 (Extraversion): scored = 6 − q15_value Q16 (Neuroticism): scored = 6 − q16_value
Dimension calculations (after reverse transforms): ocean_openness: (q1 + q2 + (6−q13)) / 3 ocean_conscientiousness: (q3 + q4 + (6−q14)) / 3 ocean_extraversion: (q5 + q6 + (6−q15)) / 3 ocean_agreeableness: (q7 + q8 + (6−q9)) / 3 ocean_neuroticism: (q10 + q11 + q12 + (6−q16)) / 4
All five calculations go in a single ‘Make changes to current User’ action. Use Bubble’s ‘rounded to’ operator on the final division result only.
RESPONSE PATTERN CHECK: Before writing scores, check if all 16 raw answers fall within a 2-point band (all between 4–5, or all between 1–2, etc.). If yes, set User.ocean_profile_flagged = Yes. Do not block the user or show an error. Append this line to the standing context block in all prompts when the flag is true: ‘Note: OCEAN response pattern was narrow — treat scores as lower-confidence prior.’
Individual question scores as named fields (q1_score, q2_score, etc.)

All raw answers are in personality_profile_json. Named per-question fields would create 12 redundant fields that are never read by routing logic. If granular reanalysis is needed in future, parse the JSON.
Labels are interpretive and may change as the scoring model evolves. Only raw scores are stored. Labels are generated at runtime from score ranges when needed.

The system does not categorise users into personality types. It uses the five individual dimension scores as continuous context. Type labels would lose information and create routing shortcuts we explicitly want to avoid.

The OCEAN assessment runs again at Day 90 and every 90 days thereafter. Scores are not replaced — they are blended into a running average across all assessments. This means a single reassessment cannot dramatically shift the profile; the profile converges toward a stable true value over time.

assessment_count starts at 1 after onboarding. Increments by 1 after each reassessment. After 3 assessments, each contributes equal weight (33.3%). This field must be read before writing new blended scores and incremented atomically in the same workflow action.
New fields required on User record

Number. Integer. Starts at 1 after onboarding assessment. Increments by 1 after each 90-day reassessment. Used in the running average formula. Must be incremented in the same atomic write as the updated scores.

Date. Set to current date after each assessment (onboarding and reassessment). Used to calculate when the next reassessment is due: ocean_last_assessed + 90 days. When this date is in the past and the user opens the app, the Day 90 reassessment prompt fires.
Yes/No. Default No. Set to Yes if the response pattern check (Section 3.2) detects a narrow band. Used to append a low-confidence note to AI standing context. Resets to No after a clean reassessment.

Long Text. JSON array. Each entry is the raw answer set from one assessment plus a timestamp and the dimension scores calculated from that sitting. Format: [{"date":"2024-01-15","scores":{"q1":4,...,"q16":2},"dimensions":{"O":3.7,"C":4.0,"E":2.0,"A":2.3,"N":3.8}}, ...]. Append-only — never overwrite. Exists for longitudinal analysis and quality review. Not read by any AI prompt or routing logic.

When the user opens the app and ocean_last_assessed + 90 days is in the past, intercept the normal Day entry flow and show the OCEAN assessment screens again (same 16 questions, same layout, no explanation). Do not tell the user it is a reassessment. Do not tell the user their previous scores. The prompt simply appears — identical to onboarding — before they reach the entry screen.

DEVELOPER NOTE After the 16th answer is submitted: (1) calculate the 5 new dimension scores from this sitting. (2) Read current assessment_count. (3) Apply the running average formula to each dimension score. (4) Write the 5 updated blended scores, the incremented assessment_count, and the updated ocean_last_assessed date in one atomic action. (5) Append the raw sitting data to ocean_profile_json_history. (6) Fire the personality summary API call with the new blended scores. (7) Overwrite personality_summary_text with the new summary. All of steps 1–5 must complete before step 6 fires. Steps 6–7 can fail without blocking the user — apply the same 8-second timeout and fallback logic from Section 2.3.

After a reassessment, show the Summary Screen once with the new personality_summary_text. Exact copy change from onboarding: replace ‘Here’s what we noticed.’ with ‘Here’s what we’re seeing now.’ Everything else is identical. The user taps Continue and enters the normal day flow.
4. How It Is Used for Analysis and Interpretation

The OCEAN data does two distinct things in the system: it generates a one-time personality summary shown to the user at onboarding, and it provides standing context passed silently into every AI prompt the platform generates for that user's entire program.

One API call fires after Q12 is submitted. It receives all five dimension scores and returns a 2–3 sentence plain language description of how this person tends to process their inner life. This is the only time OCEAN data is directly surfaced to the user.

You are reading a person's OCEAN personality assessment scores on a scale of 1–5 where 5 is highest.
Openness: [ocean_openness] | Conscientiousness: [ocean_conscientiousness] | Extraversion: [ocean_extraversion] | Agreeableness: [ocean_agreeableness] | Neuroticism: [ocean_neuroticism]
Write 2–3 plain sentences describing how this person tends to process their inner life. Do not use OCEAN terminology or clinical language. Do not mention scores or numbers. Write it the way you would describe someone to a new person who is about to interact with them.
End with one sentence that begins: 'This space is designed for exactly that.'
Example output: 'You tend to process things internally and find direct conflict uncomfortable. That means things often pile up quietly before they surface. This space is designed for exactly that.'
Be accurate. Be plain. Do not be warm or encouraging. Do not mention what the space will do for them beyond that final sentence. Just describe what you see.

These thresholds are used internally by the AI prompt context — they are not surfaced to the user and not stored as separate fields. They are documented here so the logic can be reviewed and adjusted if scoring changes.
What it signals to the AI
User tends toward certainty-seeking. Reflections should be more concrete and grounded — avoid abstract reframing. Exercises should name the specific thing, not the pattern.
User is open to examining their own role. Reflections can go deeper faster. Less scaffolding needed before the honest observation.
Habit formation is not automatic for this user. The daily entry practice may need more consistent nudging. Exercise framing should not feel like a task or homework.
Internal processor. Never assume talking to someone is the natural next step. 'Have you talked to anyone about this?' is a tone-deaf prompt for this user.

Conflict avoidance is likely present. When entries describe interpersonal tension, reflections should probe the avoidance gently. High agreeableness + high PR in Day 30 assessment = strong Branch C or A signal.
Emotionally reactive, ruminative. Reflections should not amplify distress — name what is there, don't dwell. High neuroticism + worsening DT = close monitoring flag.
Emotionally stable. Reflections can be more direct. Less need for attentive framing around distress signals.
4.3 Standing Context Block — Passed Into All Subsequent AI Prompts

From Day 1 onwards, every AI prompt the platform generates includes the following standing context block. It appears before the user's entry content in all daily reflection prompts, exercise analysis prompts, and report generation prompts. It is never shown to the user.
STANDING CONTEXT BLOCK — PREPENDED TO ALL AI PROMPTS AFTER ONBOARDING

Personality context (do not surface to user — use to calibrate tone and framing only): [personality_summary_text]
OCEAN scores: Openness [score] | Conscientiousness [score] | Extraversion [score] | Agreeableness [score] | Neuroticism [score]

This context shapes tone without being cited. The AI does not say 'because you are highly agreeable' — it simply adjusts how it frames observations about conflict avoidance. The user experiences this as the platform responding accurately to them, not as a profile being applied to them.
How it adjusts AI behaviour — examples

Daily reflections probe withheld feelings more gently. Exercise prompts that ask about conflict name the cost of avoidance without prescribing confrontation. The Avoidance Audit (Ex 6A) and Unfinished Conversation exercises feel more resonant because the framing already assumes something is being held back.

Reflections never suggest 'talking to someone' as a first response. Exercise framing doesn't assume social support is available or wanted. The platform meets the user where processing actually happens — internally.
Reflections name what is present without amplifying it. The tone is more careful around distress language. The platform does not pile more onto what is already heavy.
Re-engagement prompts (3-day absence email) are warmer and more curious, less task-oriented. Exercise framing avoids language that sounds like homework or self-improvement obligation.
Reflections can go deeper sooner. Less scaffolding. The platform trusts the user to sit with an uncomfortable observation without needing it softened first.
4.4 OCEAN x Emotion Language — Weekly Report Word Family Feed

The weekly report Emotion Language This Week section shows words the user actually wrote, mapped to related words in the same family they didn't use. OCEAN context shapes which unused words are surfaced and how the observation is framed.

Words like tired, stressed, fine in entries are more likely to be read as deflections — the AI surfaces higher-intensity related words (e.g. tired → exhausted, depleted) because the neuroticism profile supports the inference that the surface word is understating what is present.
The same surface words are less likely to be treated as deflections. Tired may just mean tired. The AI is less aggressive about surfacing heavier related words.

When conflict-adjacent words appear (frustrated, disappointed, irritated), the AI surfaces the stronger related words — resentful, bitter — because high agreeableness users are more likely to understate relational frustration.
The AI maps to concrete, situational related words rather than abstract ones. Low-openness users need concrete grounding, not expanded abstraction.

No additional API call or field is needed for this. The OCEAN standing context block is already in the weekly report prompt. The word family mapping is handled entirely within that prompt. OCEAN context adjusts which related words are prioritised and how the observation is framed.
4.5 OCEAN x Branch Routing — Interaction Table

OCEAN scores are not routing inputs — branch routing is driven by EI, PR, SA, DT scores from entries. But when the Day 30 and monthly reports explain branch patterns narratively, the OCEAN profile gives the dispositional context that makes the pattern make sense.
How AI uses it in reports
The entrenched pattern is likely organised around relational harmony — avoiding conflict, maintaining surface stability. Rigidity is protective of connection, not just habit.
Reports frame the pattern as relational protection. The pattern keeps things smooth on the surface rather than the pattern keeps repeating.
Strong prior for why suppression exists — emotional content is withheld to avoid burdening others or disrupting relationships. Most common and coherent combination in the system.
Reports are more confident naming the relational cost of suppression. Body Signal Inventory and Recurring Scenario exercises are framed around what is being absorbed for others comfort.
OCEAN confirms the branch — this user experiences emotions intensely by disposition, not just situationally. Branch assignment is structurally sound.
Reports can be more direct about intensity as a stable characteristic rather than a situational reaction.
Emotionally reactive + low sense of authorship = high risk of overwhelm when exercises surface difficult patterns. Pacing matters more.
Monthly reports are more careful about how much is named at once. Exercise framing is warmer throughout.
Daily entry habit is at higher risk of dropout. Exercises may take longer to unlock because entry count grows more slowly.
Re-engagement framing is warmer throughout. Monthly reports never reference missed entries as failure.
Double rigidity signal — dispositional resistance to reframing plus entrenched behavioural patterns. This user will resist Cost-Benefit Audit reframing most strongly.
Reports are more concrete and less abstract. Reframing is introduced more gradually.
Seemingly contradictory — willing to examine their own role but not crediting themselves with agency. Often indicates intellectual self-awareness without behavioural follow-through.
Reports name the gap between understanding and action directly.
4.6 Fallback — Exact Text When personality_summary_text Is Empty

If the API call that generates personality_summary_text fails or times out at onboarding, the field will be empty. Every AI prompt template has a [PERSONALITY_CONTEXT] placeholder. This placeholder must resolve to something usable — not blank, not an error.
FALLBACK TEXT FOR [PERSONALITY_CONTEXT] WHEN PERSONALITY_SUMMARY_TEXT IS EMPTY

Personality context: No summary available. Use OCEAN scores for calibration only. Openness [score] | Conscientiousness [score] | Extraversion [score] | Agreeableness [score] | Neuroticism [score]. Calibration: Openness < 2.5 = certainty-seeking; Agreeableness >= 3.5 = conflict-avoidant; Neuroticism >= 3.5 = emotionally reactive; Extraversion < 2.5 = internal processor; Conscientiousness < 2.5 = habit formation at risk. SCORE FORMAT: Replace each [score] placeholder with the stored field value formatted to one decimal place (e.g. 3.5, not 3.50 and not 3). All five OCEAN fields are stored to one decimal place as specified in Section 3.1 â use that stored value directly without reformatting.

Build this as a conditional in the prompt template construction logic. Pseudocode: if User.personality_summary_text is not empty → use summary + OCEAN scores line. Else → use fallback text with raw scores. This conditional runs every time a prompt is assembled — not once at onboarding. It handles the empty-summary case permanently without requiring a retry workflow.
The personality summary shown to the user uses second-person you language — You tend to process things internally. This is a deliberate decision held consistently across the system.
CHOSEN. The platform speaks to the user as someone capable of handling what is true. Starting with you at onboarding establishes this register immediately.
Rejected. Third person is appropriate for the internal standing context block — not for user-facing copy on the Summary Screen.
Rejected. Generalising softens the observation and reduces the chance the user feels accurately seen.

Consistency rule: personality_summary_text stored on the User record is always second-person you language. The standing context block passed into AI prompts rephrases this to third-person this person language for internal AI use. The stored field is always in you voice — the Summary Screen renders it directly without transformation.

The AI prompt in Section 4.1 already specifies you language via the example output. If the AI returns third-person language, retry once. If retry also fails, use the fallback from Section 4.6. A simple check: if the returned summary does not begin with You, treat it as a failed response. TIMEOUT BUDGET: The retry shares the original 8-second budget (Section 2.3) â it is not a fresh 8-second window. Both the first attempt and the retry must complete within the same 8-second timeout that started when the API call was initiated. Do not restart the timer on retry. FIELD WRITE RULE: If both attempts fail the You check, do not write any text to personality_summary_text. Leave the field empty. The Section 4.6 fallback is applied at prompt-assembly time (every time a prompt is built), not at onboarding write time. Writing fallback text to the stored field would make it permanent and uncorrectable â the intent is for the field to reflect a real AI-generated summary or nothing.
5. How It Feeds Into Weekly and Monthly Reports

The OCEAN assessment does not generate a section in the weekly report. It is not mentioned to the user after the summary screen. What it does is act as invisible infrastructure — it shapes every report the platform generates without ever being named.
The weekly report (Pattern Summary) does not reference OCEAN directly. However, the OCEAN standing context block is passed into the AI prompt that generates the following weekly report sections:

The one-sentence week tone description is calibrated to the user's processing style. A high-neuroticism user's 'heavier' week is described with more care. A high-openness user's week can be named more directly.

The primary AI narrative paragraph. OCEAN context prevents the AI from making assumptions that don't fit — e.g. not framing isolation as unusual for a low-extraversion user, or not interpreting emotional flatness as suppression for a low-neuroticism user when it may just be their baseline.
The contextual framing paragraph. OCEAN adjusts what 'matters' is pointed at — for a high-agreeableness user, the significance of a withheld feeling is different than for a low-agreeableness user.
The pointed question. OCEAN shapes what kind of question lands — abstract for high-openness users, concrete and situational for low-openness users.

If an exercise was completed that week, the exercise summary in the weekly report is framed against the OCEAN profile. 'You ranked Peace as your top value' lands differently for a high-agreeableness user — the AI names the connection.

The OCEAN standing context block is prepended to the weekly report AI prompt — it is not a separate API call. It is simply included in the prompt alongside the week's entry content. The prompt template has a [PERSONALITY_CONTEXT] placeholder that is filled from User.personality_summary_text and the five ocean_ fields at runtime.
Same pattern as weekly — OCEAN is not named, not cited, not surfaced. It is standing context in the monthly report AI prompt. Its influence is most visible in two monthly report sections:

When explaining a SA score or DT trajectory, the AI adjusts language based on OCEAN profile. A low-extraversion user with low SA is described differently than a high-extraversion user with the same score — the source of the agency deficit is likely different.

When the monthly report tracks exercise outputs — is the Avoidance Audit avoidance still present? Is the Cost-Benefit pattern still deploying? — the OCEAN profile gives the AI context for why the pattern persists. High agreeableness + persistent avoidance reads differently than low agreeableness + persistent avoidance.
Tone calibration across the whole report
High neuroticism users receive a monthly report that is careful not to amplify distress. Low conscientiousness users receive one that doesn't frame non-completion of exercises as failure.

The OCEAN profile is passed into the Day 30 report generation prompt as standing context. It does not generate a section of its own. Its primary influence at Day 30 is on how the four dimension scores are interpreted — the same EI score of 7 reads differently against a high-neuroticism baseline than against a low-neuroticism baseline.

High Agreeableness (≥ 3.5) is not a routing input on its own — branch routing is driven by EI, PR, SA, DT scores from entries. But when the Day 30 report narratively explains a Branch A or C routing decision, the AI can reference agreeableness as a contributing disposition that makes sense of the pattern — without calling it agreeableness. 'You tend to absorb difficulty rather than name it' is the agreeableness context showing up in plain language.

The 12 questions appear in a fixed sequence, interleaved across dimensions so no two consecutive questions share a dimension. Order: O C E A N O C E A N O C E A N N (q1, q3, q5, q7, q10, q2, q4, q6, q8, q11, q13, q14, q15, q9, q12, q16). This prevents users from pattern-matching which trait is being assessed and adjusting their answers accordingly. They are not randomised per session

Store question order as a fixed constant in the codebase — not in the database. If question order ever needs to change for a future cohort, it changes in code, not in data. Do not build a 'question sequence' table in Bubble.

Several questions — particularly Q7, Q8, Q9 (Agreeableness) and Q10–12 (Neuroticism) — are likely to attract socially desirable responses. Users may select 1 or 2 for Q8 ('I often say I'm fine when I'm not') because admitting this feels like a weakness at first contact with a new product.

The design mitigation is structural, not instructional: one question per screen with no visible dimension labels reduces the sense that the user is being scored. The auto-advance after selection reduces deliberation time. No 'Are you sure?' confirmation step. The goal is to capture the instinctive response, not the considered one.

Do not include any instructional text that says 'answer honestly' or 'there are no right or wrong answers.' This instruction is counterproductive — it signals that the platform expects deception and invites the user to perform honesty rather than just respond.

OCEAN scores from a 12-question self-report are indicative, not diagnostic. The system treats them as a starting calibration that can be implicitly updated over time as journal entries reveal a more accurate picture. If a user scores low on Neuroticism at onboarding but their first 10 entries show high emotional reactivity, the AI will observe this — not by overriding the OCEAN score but by weighting entry evidence more heavily than the onboarding profile as the program progresses.

The OCEAN score is a prior. The entries are the evidence. As evidence accumulates, the prior matters less. This is not built as explicit logic — it is a consequence of how the AI prompt is constructed: entry content comes after the OCEAN context block, and AI models naturally weight more recent, specific, concrete information over abstract background context.

If a user begins the assessment but does not tap an answer for 15 minutes, the in-progress session is silently discarded on their next interaction and the assessment restarts from Q1 with a clean answer set. No error is shown. This prevents partial or stale answer sets from corrupting scores.

Implementation: store assessment_started_at (ISO timestamp) on the User record when the assessment begins. Reset it on each answer tap. On every tap and navigation event during the assessment, check elapsed time. If elapsed > 15 minutes: clear answers, reset assessment_started_at to null, restart from Q1. Clear assessment_started_at to null on successful completion (after scores are written).
6.4 What Happens If a User Drops Mid-Assessment

personality_profile_json is NOT written (it only writes after Q12). No partial data is stored. When user returns, the gate condition (personality_profile_json is empty) is still true — assessment restarts from Q1. Do not attempt to resume mid-assessment.
User drops after Q12 but before API call completes

personality_profile_json IS written (fires immediately on Q12 submission). Five dimension scores ARE written. personality_summary_text is NOT written (API didn't complete). When user returns: gate condition (personality_profile_json is empty) is FALSE — assessment does not restart. User is routed to Day 1 entry screen. personality_summary_text will remain empty. The standing context block in subsequent AI prompts will use the five ocean_ score fields directly, not the summary text, as fallback.
User drops after API completes but before tapping Continue

personality_summary_text IS written. onboarding_completed is NOT yet Yes. When user returns: gate condition is false (profile_json exists). Show Summary Screen again with the stored personality_summary_text — this is the one exception to the one-time rule. The user didn't see it complete. Once they tap Continue, onboarding_completed = Yes and they never see it again.

The fallback for missing personality_summary_text must be handled in every AI prompt template. If personality_summary_text is empty, the prompt should use the five ocean_ scores directly with a simplified framing line rather than failing or passing empty context. Build this fallback into the prompt template, not as a separate workflow.

The OCEAN assessment is not designed to be repeated. However, if a second cycle begins (Day 31+), there may be value in a silent background recalibration — not a repeat of the 12-question assessment, but an AI inference of personality profile shift based on 30 days of entry evidence. This is not built in v1 and should not be over-engineered now. The architecture supports it: if ocean_ fields are updated on the User record, all downstream prompts automatically receive the updated context. The question of when and whether to update is a product decision for after launch.
